newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers intensify protest, block fuel.
newsitem.headline: French truckers intensify protest, block fuel.

text.p: Truck drivers blocked roads across France for the third successive day on Wednesday and vowed to blockade fuel depots and cut supplies to supermarkets to press their demands for wage rises and shorter working hours.

Thousands of trucks barricaded roads and motorways in some 38 locations around the country and thousands more stood idle on parking lots, raising fears of repeat of a 1992 truckers' blockade that paralysed France in a traffic nightmare.
"The truckers are really angry. They are tired, they have no money and no family life. They are exhausted at 40," a spokesman for the Communist-led CGT trade union said.

As the government urged employers to negotiate, unions vowed to step up their protest. It spread to Paris, which had been spared so far, and lorries started blocking traffic on the motorway around the capital.
After another failed round of talks with employers, drivers had earlier begun preventing tankers leaving oil refineries, to cut supplies to petrol stations.
Depots were blocked in Bordeaux and Caen. The major Royal Dutch/Shell refinery of Berre near Marseille was also cut off but a spokesman said refinery operations continued normally.
A spokeswoman for the powerful National Truck Drivers Federation (FNCR), said petrol stations and supermarkets kept low stocks and the blockade could bite within 48 hours.

Truckers have singled out Bordeaux, whose mayor is Prime Minister Alain Juppe, as the main focus of protests, causing huge traffic jams on all access roads. Airlines at Bordeaux airport said air freight was badly hit.
A CGT spokesman acknowledged the protest was getting out of unions' control, with many truckers acting on their own. "Don't you think we are controlling every roadblock," he said.

There were roadblocks in the south near Toulouse, on the A9 motorway to Spain between Nimes and Montpellier and near Avignon, in the west around Caen, Le Mans and Rennes and on the motorway between Paris and Rouen.
Lyon in the centre and Lille in the north were also hit.
In the east, truckers lifted a three-day blockade of Strasbourg's Europe Bridge between France and Germany and went on to cut off the motorway to Paris.
Unions said protesters were letting firemen, ambulances and doctors pass. Private cars were also allowed to trickle through but trucks were stopped whether they joined the protests or not.

Unions said they were trying to force the government to put pressure on employers to make concessions. Transport Minister Bernard Pons summoned haulage bosses to a meeting at 1630 GMT in order to "notify them...he wished a negotiated settlement to the dispute to be found as soon as possible".

The spreading paralysis recalled the truckers' 10-day protest in 1992 which turned a July holiday rush into a nightmare for hundreds of thousands of tourists stranded on highways as police tried in vain to remove blockading trucks.
That action was triggered by a planned new points system for driving licences, although it grew into a conflict over general working conditions.

The government eventually agreed to soften the points system and promised drivers greater protection from employers who made them exceed contractual working hours and break speed limits to meet delivery deadlines.
The six unions backing the current protest say promises have not been kept. They are demanding big wage rises, shorter working hours and the right for drivers to retire at 55 instead of 60.
